kit.item: Make the low-carbon option the one people get unless they choose otherwise
kit.example: "Your plan is renewable power at the same price. Switch any time."
kit.effect: 62 points more green contracts; 31 to 47 points more plant-based meals
kit.fails: The choice at one counter or form, not what people eat all day. Weaker as the price or the effort to opt out rises.
kit.cite: Ebeling and Lotz 2015; Fowlie et al. 2021; Boronowsky et al. 2022

kit.item: Add low-carbon dishes, and keep the others
kit.example: "Half the mains are plant-based, and the burger is still there."
kit.effect: 8 to 22 points more vegetarian meals sold
kit.fails: Only where the dishes are good and actually served. Eighteen worksites that partly made the change moved 2.3 points, not significant.
kit.cite: Garnett et al. 2019; Arrazat et al. 2024; Pechey et al. 2022

kit.item: Name the dish for its taste, not for what it lacks
kit.effect: 14 percent more diners took vegetables than with plain names, 29 percent more than with health names
kit.evidence: Preregistered field study, 137,842 diner decisions, 5 US dining halls
kit.fails: Vegetables, not meat swaps. No effect at the dining hall with the least tasty food.

kit.example: "Could we skip meat two days a week?"
kit.effect: 6.9 points more meatless meals than a go-vegetarian appeal, not significant; 59 percent took the pledge, against 15 percent
kit.evidence: Preregistered field trial, 617 students, one café
kit.fails: Neither appeal beat no appeal. Fewer of those who pledged to cut back kept the pledge.

kit.item: Give the honest size of a small step
kit.example: "Green power is a good step. It covers a small part of emissions, so the larger changes still matter."
kit.effect: Support for a carbon tax fell from 70.3 to 55.0 percent when a green default was offered; one sentence on the default's small size brought it back to 72
kit.fails: Hypothetical votes, one research group. No study has measured real policy outcomes.

kit.item: Say what most people already think and do
kit.example: "Most people here want more renewable power."
kit.effect: Donations to a climate charity rose 12 dollars, 4.7 percent, when people learned that 62 percent of Americans try to fight global warming
kit.evidence: Online experiment with real money, United States
kit.fails: One study, measured at once. A norm below what the audience already does can pull them down.
kit.cite: Andre et al. (Review of Economics and Statistics); Schultz et al. 2007

kit.item: Let someone who already does it make the ask
kit.example: "We put panels on last spring. Come and see the bill."
kit.effect: Volunteers who had solar themselves recruited 62.8 percent more installations
kit.fails: One program. An activist image or a superior tone lowers willingness.

kit.item: Lead with health and comfort, not only money
kit.example: "Less standby power, cleaner air for the children in this building."
kit.effect: Health and environment messages cut electricity use 8.2 percent; cost messages saved nothing
kit.fails: One building complex. Real money still moves large purchases.

kit.item: If you name the threat, name one step in the same breath
kit.example: "The heat waves are getting worse. The boiler is the largest thing this house controls, and a grant pays half."
kit.effect: Fear appeals worked better with a step attached (d 0.43 against 0.21); in the 63-country test, no message raised the tree-planting task
kit.fails: Doom alone raised sharing and lowered effort in the tournament.
kit.cite: Tannenbaum et al. 2015; Vlasceanu et al. 2024

kit.item: Point at the large choices, and make them easy
kit.example: "One vetted installer, one price for the whole town, a free site visit."
kit.effect: 37 more solar installations per campaign town; free home retrofits went from under 1 to about 6 percent take-up
kit.evidence: Field programs and trials, Connecticut and Michigan
kit.fails: The campaign effect stopped when the campaign did. Outreach cost more than 1,000 dollars per extra home.
kit.cite: Gillingham and Bollinger 2021; Fowlie, Greenstone and Wolfram 2018

kit.item: Cut the upfront cost and the paperwork, not add facts
kit.example: "Nothing to pay upfront, and the grant forms are done for you."
kit.effect: Efficiency information alone did not change water-heater purchases; a 100-dollar rebate did
kit.evidence: Field trial, US retail call center
kit.fails: Rebates cost money per tonne. Stated-choice surveys overstate uptake.

kit.item: Compare with similar neighbors, and approve those doing well
kit.example: "You used 12 percent less than similar homes nearby." with a smiley
kit.effect: Home energy reports cut electricity use 1.3 to 2.0 percent
kit.evidence: Field trials, millions of US homes
kit.fails: Small, and smaller at scale. Low users told the average used more, unless the report added approval.

kit.item: Show the use where and when it happens
kit.example: A shower display that counts liters as the water runs
kit.effect: Shower energy fell 22 percent at home, 11.4 percent in hotels
kit.fails: The repeat with hotel guests gave half the effect.
kit.cite: Tiefenbeck et al. 2018; Tiefenbeck et al. 2019
